title: The Communication Gap Between Textile Quality Standards and Consumer Perceptions: A Comparative Qualitative Study in Bangladesh and Russia
content: Technical textile quality is expressed through laboratory indicators such as fabric strength, seam strength, colour fastness, durability, dimensional stability, and abrasion resistance, yet consumers usually judge apparel through cues that are visible, tactile, experiential, or brand-related. This study examines the Textile Quality Communication Gap: the difference between technical quality information produced by textile and apparel professionals and consumers’ ability to understand and use it. Fifty semi-structured interviews were conducted in Bangladesh and Russia with 30 apparel consumers, 10 textile professionals, and 10 marketing or brand professionals. Ethics approval was obtained and all participants gave informed verbal consent. Thematic analysis identified five themes. Consumers relied mainly on fabric feel, appearance, finishing, price, brand reputation, and previous experience; many found technical terminology difficult to interpret; and their descriptions did not always match professional language. Technical information became more useful when translated into practical benefits. Clear communication was associated with consumer confidence and perceived brand credibility, and consistency between claims and performance was emphasised. Shared patterns appeared in both countries, alongside context-specific differences: proximity to garment manufacturing in Bangladesh and post-sanction market shifts in Russia. The study offers a communication-centred account of the link between objective and perceived quality. For managers, the findings support translating technical terms into concrete benefits, avoiding vague claims, and aligning communication with actual product performance.
